title: Whose is it?
seoTitle: Turkish genitive case (-ın, -in): whose is it?
intro: [Unit 9](a1-u09) gave nouns an owner with a suffix: *evim* (my house), *evi* (his house). This unit names the owner. The genitive `-(n)In` turns a name or a noun into an owner, *Ayşe'nin* (Ayşe's), *evin* (of the house), and the owned thing keeps its possessive: *Ayşe'nin evi*, *evin kapısı* (the door of the house). You'll also meet *benim, senin, onun*, the n in *evinde* (at his house), and the questions *Kimin?* (whose?) and *Kimde?* (who has it?).

blocks.text: The genitive (*ilgi hâli*) marks the owner, like **'s** or **of** in English. After a consonant it is `-In`, in four-way harmony: *evin* (of the house), *okulun* (of the school), *Mehmet'in* (Mehmet's). After a vowel a buffer n comes first: *arabanın* (of the car), *Ayşe'nin* (Ayşe's).

**Softening and vowel loss.** After a consonant the genitive starts with a vowel, so it brings out the same changes as the possessive of [unit 9](gp-possessive-softening): *kitabın* (of the book), *çocuğun* (the child's), *ağacın* (of the tree), *şehrin* (of the city), *oğlun* (the son's). *Su* takes a y: *suyun*. Names keep their consonant and their apostrophe: *Mehmet'in*, *Burak'ın*.
**Pronouns.** The personal pronouns have their own genitive, and two of them are irregular: *benim* and *bizim* end in `-Im`, not `-In`.

The demonstratives take the n you met on *onda* in [unit 5](gp-pronoun-n): *bunun* (of this), *şunun* (of that), *onun*. The question word *kim* gives *kimin* (whose), the subject of the last section of this guide.
A genitive can also stand alone as the predicate, like **mine** or **Ayşe's**: *Bu kitap benim* (This book is mine).
*Benin* and *bizin* don't exist: **my** is *benim*, **our** is *bizim*. And after a vowel, don't forget the n: *arabanın*, not *arabaın*; *Ayşe'nin*, not *Ayşe'in*.

A possessive phrase (*belirtili isim tamlaması*) has two suffixes: the genitive on the owner and the possessive of [unit 9](gp-possessive-suffixes) on the owned thing. When the owner is a noun or a name, the owned thing takes the third person, `-(s)I`: *Ayşe'nin evi* (Ayşe's house), *Mehmet'in arabası* (Mehmet's car), *evin kapısı* (the door of the house).
**With pronouns**, the owned thing takes the owner's own person, so both words say who it belongs to: *benim evim* (my house), *senin araban* (your car), *bizim mahallemiz* (our neighbourhood).

**Dropping the pronoun.** The suffix on the owned thing already says who the owner is, so the pronoun is usually left out, just as subject pronouns are: *Evim büyük* (My house is big). Keep it for emphasis or contrast: *Benim evim büyük, senin evin küçük* (**My** house is big, **yours** is small). A noun or a name can't be dropped: *Ayşe'nin evi*.

**Their.** After *onların*, the owned thing usually takes the plain third person: *onların evi* (their house). Without *onların*, use `-lArI`: *evleri* (their house), as in [unit 9](gp-possessive-suffixes).

**To have, with a named owner.** *Arabası var* (She has a car) from [unit 9](gp-possessive-have) can now name the owner: *Ayşe'nin arabası var* (Ayşe has a car), *Mehmet'in köpeği yok* (Mehmet doesn't have a dog).

items.en: The door of the building is open.
Our neighbour's dog is in the garden.
Ayşe's mother's house is in Izmir.
items.note: a chain: *annesi* takes a genitive too, with the n of the next section

blocks.text: English has two patterns, **Ayşe's house** and **the door of the house**, and French puts the owner last: la porte de la maison. Turkish has one pattern, with the owner always first: *Ayşe'nin evi*, *evin kapısı*.

Both suffixes are needed: *Ayşe'nin ev* and *Ayşe ev* are wrong. Without the genitive, two nouns make a compound of a different kind, *ev kapısı* (a house door, a front door), which comes in [A2](gp-compound-indefinite).

In everyday speech, *bizim* and *sizin* often appear without the suffix on the owned thing: *bizim ev* (our house), *bizim mahalle* (our neighbourhood). In writing, and in this course, use *bizim evimiz* or just *evimiz*.

sections.title: Evinde, arabasına: the n before a case ending

blocks.text: When a case ending follows the third-person possessive `-(s)I` or `-lArI`, an n slips in between: *evi* (his house) → *evinde* (in his house), *evine* (to his house), *evinden* (from his house), *evini* (his house, as an object). This pronominal n (*zamir n'si*) is the n you met on *onda* and *ona* in [unit 5](gp-pronoun-n).

The n replaces the buffer y: the dative is *-nA* (*arabasına*, not *arabasıya*) and the accusative *-nI* (*arabasını*). It comes only after the third person, singular or plural: *evlerinde* (in their house), *arabalarına* (to their car). The other persons take the case directly: *evimde*, *evimizde*, *arabanıza*.

items.en: There's a garden at Ayşe's house.
She's closing the door of her room.
We're staying at her mother's house.
The neighbours are drinking tea on their balconies.

blocks.text: *Evinde* can mean **in your house** (*ev-in-de*) or **in his house** (*ev-i-n-de*): the two read the same. The pronoun or the context tells them apart: *Senin evinde mi?* (At your place?) *Hayır, onun evinde.* (No, at his.) After a vowel they differ: *arabanda* (in your car), *arabasında* (in his car).
The same n appears on many words that end in a third-person possessive, as you'll see with compounds in A2: whenever a case ending follows `-(s)I`, expect an n.

sections.title: Kimin? Kimde? Whose is it, who has it?

blocks.text: *Kimin* is the genitive of *kim*: **whose**. Put it before the owned thing, *Kimin çantası?* (Whose bag?), or use it as the predicate: *Bu çanta kimin?* (Whose bag is this?) The answer is a genitive too, often on its own: *Benim.* (It's mine.) *Ayşe'nin.* (It's Ayşe's.)

items.en: Whose car is in the garden?
Is it yours? No, it isn't mine.
Who is the owner of this house?

blocks.text: *Kimde* is the locative of *kim*. With people, the locative means **has it on them**, as in *Anahtar bende* (I've got the key) from [unit 5](gp-pronoun-n). So *kimin* asks who owns something, and *kimde* who is holding it right now. *Kimde* also asks who has one at all: *Kimde kalem var?* (Who has a pen?)

lines.en: I don't have it. Does Murat have it?

lines.tr: Evet, bende. Araba benim değil, Selin'in.
lines.en: Yes, I've got it. The car isn't mine, it's Selin's.

blocks.text: *Kitap Ayşe'de* means Ayşe has the book, perhaps one she borrowed; *Kitap Ayşe'nin* means the book belongs to her. Keep the n of the genitive apart from the d of the locative.

summary: The genitive `-(n)In` marks the owner: *evin, okulun, arabanın, Ayşe'nin*. It softens like the possessive: *kitabın, çocuğun*; *su* gives *suyun*.
Pronouns: *benim, senin, onun, bizim, sizin, onların*, and *bunun, şunun, kimin*. *Benim* and *bizim* are irregular.
A possessive phrase needs both suffixes: *Ayşe'nin evi, evin kapısı, benim evim*. Drop a pronoun owner unless it is stressed: *evim*.
A named owner can **have** things: *Ayşe'nin arabası var*.
After the third-person possessive, case endings take an n: *evinde, evine, evinden, evini; arabasına*.
*Kimin?* asks who owns it, *Kimde?* who has it: *Bu kimin? Benim.* *Anahtar kimde? Bende.*
